newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong stock exchange outlines 1997 plans.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong stock exchange outlines 1997 plans.

text.p: Hong Kong's outgoing stock exchange chief gave a full list of tasks to the incoming chief executive on Thursday, including development of new products and technological enhancements to the exchange's trading systems.

"In the coming year, technology, globalisation, the China market and whether Hong Kong will maintain its openness are the key issues," Paul Chow, chief executive of the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong Ltd, said at a year-end news conference.
Chow will leave his post on January 31 and hand the reins to Alec Tsui, currently the deputy chief executive.

Chow said the exchange would seek to enhance the efficiency and sophistication of the local stock market with the introduction of new products, which were under review by the New Market Development Working Group.
Another group within the exchange, the China Working Group, was looking into ways to help the exchange become a major trading centre in overseas listed China stocks, said Chow.
In the past three years, the exchange had listed 22 H shares, Chow said. Shandong Xinhua Pharmaceutical Co Ltd will list before the end of the month, bringing the total to 23.
Five H-share companies were listed in 1996, raising a total of HK$6.56 billion, Chow said.
Chow said he hopes to see the exchange bring the number to 50 by 2000.
"In this way we would have created a critical mass, secured ourselves as the major listing and trading centre of Chinese equities outside of China," he said.

Another goal in 1997 was to improve coordination between the stock and futures exchanges by cross margining and other means, Chow said, adding that the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) was taking part in the discussions.
The exchange will also seek ways to increase the market's appeal to retail investors, he said.
"In October, about 35 percent of turnover was derived from the retail sector and about 40 percent in November," he said.
In another move to improve trading efficiency, the exchange will issue a consultation paper, probably in the first quarter of 1997, to the brokerage community.
Included in the paper will be recommendations on computer-to-computer trading systems, removing restrictions on odd lot trading and eliminating restrictions on executing two price queues, he said.
Beginning in early January, the exchange will issue all information in both Chinese and English. On January 2, the exchange will launch its Web site on the Internet.
The exchange is reviewing the brokerage commission, custody and registration fee and the level of the stamp duty, a tax paid to the government on each stock market transaction.
Chow said the exchange would also seek to enhance its relationship with the Chinese markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen.
Chow said the exchange's most significant achievement in 1996 was the establishment of off-floor trading.
He said 50 percent of the exchange's turnover was traded outside the trading hall and that the second terminal has allowed exchange members to increase their business.
As of mid-December, 804 second terminals were installed in brokers' offices, allowing brokers to deal in listed securities without going to the trading floor.
